labels.running:
Stab wound: tamponade, PEA and pericardiocentesis
Choose another scenario
A 30-year-old man with a stab wound to the left chest. He arrives tachycardic, with a narrow pulse pressure and a raised CVP; blood is collecting in the pericardium. Without drainage he loses his pulse (PEA) about 8 minutes after arrival. CPR alone cannot bring him back; pericardiocentesis during good CPR brings the pulse back about a minute and a half later.
Arrival: tachycardic, narrow pulse pressure, raised CVP
Deteriorating: systolic below 80
Propofol 2 mg/kg given: compensation lost
PEA: organised rhythm, no pulse; the pericardium holds about 370 mL
PEA after propofol: organised rhythm, no pulse
CPR, ventilated with FiO₂ 1.0
CPR: epinephrine 1 mg given
CPR: epinephrine 1 mg repeated
CPR: pericardium drained, catheter left in
CPR, drained: epinephrine 1 mg given
Return of circulation: ventilated, catheter in the pericardium
Post-ROSC: 500 mL crystalloid running
Post-ROSC: catheter aspirated
Pericardium drained before the arrest, catheter left in
Catheter aspirated again
